entities.name: The Indic Vedic & Upanishadic Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Indic Vedic & Upanishadic Corpus constitutes the foundational sacred literature of Hinduism, classified as Shruti ("that which is heard") — considered eternal, uncreated, and divinely revealed to the ancient rishis (seers). This vast corpus comprises four layers: (1) the Samhitas — the four Vedas proper (Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda) containing hymns, sacrificial formulas, chants, and incantations; (2) the Brahmanas — prose commentaries on ritual performance; (3) the Aranyakas — "forest texts" bridging ritual and philosophy; and (4) the Upanishads — philosophical dialogues exploring the nature of Brahman (ultimate reality), Atman (the self), karma, samsara, and moksha (liberation).

The Rigveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE) is among the oldest religious texts in any Indo-European language. The Upanishads (c. 800–200 BCE) represent one of humanity's greatest philosophical achievements, influencing not only all subsequent Indian philosophy but also Western thinkers from Schopenhauer to Emerson. The entire corpus was preserved through an astonishingly precise oral tradition — one of the most remarkable feats of human memory.
